title: Sensing, Traffic, and Construction in Termites
authors: Yufei Xiao, Qinglin Wu, Kukhyun Lim, Nan-Yao Su, Paul Bardunias, Atanu Chatterjee, Saad Bhamla
abstract: Subterranean and mound-building termites excavate, transport, and build within the same granular substrate that later regulates how they sense, move, and deposit material. From antennal-scale contacts through body-scale traffic to meter-scale architecture, this review synthesizes three linked problems: how workers sense local geometry and physical cues during search and excavation; how traffic moves through narrow, evolving conduits; and how excavation and deposition remodel the substrate that guides later behavior. Across these length scales, noisy local interactions couple sensing, transport, and construction through a shared material medium, leading to emergent order at the colony scale. We emphasize what is established experimentally, where evidence remains sparse or limited to a few model systems, and how emerging imaging, tracking, and modeling tools are making these feedbacks quantitatively accessible. We use this synthesis to motivate a quantitative physics-of-life framework for termite colonies that continually rewrite the medium through which they sense, move, and build.
summary: This review synthesizes how termites manage complex tasks like foraging and building in soil whose properties are constantly altered by their own activities. It frames this as a coupled problem of sensing, traffic flow, and material deposition across vast scales. The work proposes a quantitative physics-of-life framework to model these self-organizing, adaptive subterranean ecosystems.
main_problem: The review synthesizes how three linked processes—sensing, traffic flow, and construction—interact in termite colonies to create emergent order within a shared, evolving granular medium.
main_result: Termite behavior provides a model for studying complex systems where local interactions (like tactile sensing or particle movement) continually remodel the environment that dictates future collective dynamics.
method: The paper is a comprehensive review synthesizing experimental evidence across multiple length scales, ranging from antennal contacts to meter-scale architecture.
model_or_system: The physical system is subterranean and mound-building termite colonies operating within granular substrates (soil). The model involves coupling active matter dynamics (traffic) with environmental feedback (substrate remodeling via excavation/deposition).
key_observables: Tunnel network structure, Mean Squared Displacement ($	ext{MSD}$), local geometry (curvature, roughness), moisture gradients, and path optimization rates.
important_parameters: Length scales (antennal to meter-scale), substrate properties (moisture content, grain size), and interaction types (tactile, chemical, physical).
main_assumptions: The primary framework assumes that local, noisy interactions couple sensing, transport, and construction through the shared material medium.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the coupling of information, movement, and construction across scales; detail sensing channels like antennal scanning and $	ext{MSD}$ scaling; and compare various environmental cues (moisture, airflow, chemical) influencing behavior.
paper_structure: The review is structured around synthesizing three coupled problems: 1) Sensing local geometry/cues during search/excavation; 2) Traffic movement through evolving conduits; and 3) Substrate remodeling by excavation/deposition. It emphasizes experimental findings and motivates a quantitative physics-of-life framework.
why_interesting: The concept of an environment that is dynamically rewritten by the agents moving within it—where memory, resistance, and structure are emergent variables—is highly relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and active matter theory.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Overview of the physical and behavioral themes developed in this review. (A) Schematic linking information, movement, and construction in subterranean termite colonies. (B) antennal sensing, highlighting antennation as a primary mode of local information acquisition and interaction (photo: Qinglin Wu). (C) bidirectional traffic flow through confined conduits, shown in an above-ground shelter tube (top) and a below-ground planar tunnel network (bottom) (photo: Qinglin Wu). (D) construction across scales, from above-ground shelter tubes (top, photo: Kukhyun Lim) to extended below-ground tunnel networks (bottom; photo: Paul Bardunias).

FIG. 2. Information processing in termite colonies. (A) Schematic of the coupled sensing-action loop between individual termites and the substrate they construct and inhabit. (B) Navigation. Mean squared displacement of four Cornitermes sp. workers during open-arena foraging, with MSD ∝Dτ α indicating MSD scaling [23]. For example, purple indicates α = 1.90. (C) Search. Left: Close-up of termite collective excavating tunnels [24]. Right: tunnel-tip activity and correlation between resource density and total tunnel length in C. formosanus [25]. (D) Path optimization. Left: tunnel network of C. formosanus shows pruning of long paths and reinforcement of short paths from the nest (bottom)...

FIG. 3. Traffic systems and model classes. (A) Representative traffic systems used as baselines for termite traffic: pedes- trian crowds [55], ant trails [56], and termite movement in confined galleries (Photo: Qinglin Wu). (B) Modeling descriptions arranged by scale. Social-force models represent individuals as self-driven particles with driving, interaction, wall, and noise terms. Cellular automaton models represent occupancy and probabilistic movement on a lattice. Continuum models describe density and velocity fields through conservation laws. The corresponding flux-density relations summarize how transport ca- pacity changes with density [57–61].

FIG. 4. Microscopic and macroscopic observables for confined bidirectional traffic. (A) Microscopic observables extracted from individual trajectories include the speed distribution p(v), stopping frequency and duration, and transitions among encounter, interaction, and passing states during local contact events. (B) Macroscopic observables obtained by coarse- graining trajectories include flow rate q, measured as the number of agents crossing a reference line per unit time, and density ρ, measured as the number of agents within a defined area or channel length. Filled and open circles indicate agents moving in opposite directions.

FIG. 5. Geometry-governed termite traffic. (A) Controlled tunnel manipulations show that channel width, surface irregularity, curvature, and corners alter interaction or passing time. Wider channels generally reduce encounter delays, while irregularities, curvature, and sharp corners can increase transport costs; rounding or smoothing can reduce those costs [50– 52, 70]. (B) Termite-specific features that distinguish traffic in self-built conduits: body compliance, short-range tactile sensing, and stigmergic remodeling, in which congestion can trigger construction that changes future flow.
